sweep_summary: Three sweep items for Beja (catalog: 'conflict', Almkvist 1881 weight-based vs Wedekind et al. 2008 lexical/morphemic pitch accent). Strunk 1961 is a Glottolog mis-attachment (Mycenaean Greek orthography; De Gruyter DOI; irrelevant). Vanhove 2008 (Peeters volume, HAL notice only, no file) is about intonation of converb clauses per its FR/EN abstracts, not word stress; low priority. Hudson 1973 'Syllables, moras and accents in Beja' was fetched sources in full from the author's own site (dickhudson.com; DOI 10.1017/S0022226700003534 paywalled at CUP) and read: pitch-accent system, 'the position of the accent is unpredictable', accent located 0 or 1 place (syllable, else mora) before a fixed point = last mora of the stem, the choice being lexical/grammatical, plural marked by a one-place shift; no syllable-weight placement rule. The same page yielded Hudson 1974 'A structural sketch of Beja' (African Language Studies 15), whose §1.4 states outright that accent 'is not predictable (pace Reinisch, 1893: 55 and Almkvist, 1881: 57) from its purely phonological structure' and is set by inherent final/penultimate morpheme accents within accent-units. Both files with and lines. Bearing on the catalog: refines, not resolves -- Hudson is the best first-hand statement for the lexical/morphological pole and should be added to the record (stronger than Wedekind 2008 for that side), but the weight-based readings (Almkvist, Reinisch, Vanhove 2020 §1.2) remain in the literature, so the 'conflict' code stands pending Vanhove 2017 'Le bedja' or the LangSci 603 sketch. all look-ups were done through Crossref/HAL APIs and direct fetches.

new_statements.quote: The position and nature of the realized accent is determined by the word's morphological structure, and is not predictable (pace Reinisch, 1893: 55 and Almkvist, 1881 : 57) from its purely phonological structure (e.g. /ti-rib-'a/ ' you refused ', but /ti-dif-a/ you went', whose roots belong to different accentual classes but are otherwise morphologically the same). A morpheme may or may not have an inherent accent, but if it does, there are two further variables to be specified : the position of the accentual reference-point (usually on a vowel in the last syllable of the morpheme) and the position of the accented vowel relative to this reference-point
new_statements.citation: Hudson, R. A. (1974). A structural sketch of Beja. African Language Studies 15: 111-142, §1.4 'Accent' (with Hudson, R. A. 1973, Syllables, moras and accents in Beja, Journal of Linguistics 9: 53-63, as the fuller analysis)
new_statements.reading: First-hand modern description (Hudson's own fieldwork, Port Sudan/Tokar varieties per Vanhove 2006): Beja word accent is a pitch accent whose placement is lexical-morphological, not weight-driven. Each accented morpheme carries an inherent accent of one of two types, 'final' (on its reference-point, normally the last vowel of the morpheme) or 'penultimate' (one syllable, or failing that one mora, before it); in a polymorphemic accent-unit the later inherent accent wins; plural formation typically swaps final for penultimate accent. Hudson 1973 adds that placement is counted in syllables where the accent-unit allows and in moras otherwise, that long vowels are bimoraic (level vs falling pitch), and states flatly that 'the position of the accent is unpredictable'. This is the strongest source for the lexical/morphological pole of the catalog's recorded conflict and explicitly argues against the quantity-based rules of Almkvist and Reinisch; it aligns with Wedekind et al. 2008 and Vanhove 2014 §2.4, against Vanhove 2020 §1.2. The 'conflict' code therefore stands, but Hudson 1973/1974 should be cited in the record as the primary first-hand statement for the non-weight side (it predates and is more analytically explicit than Wedekind 2008).

sources.quote: 'In Beḍawiɛt, stress is frequently very elusive. The trouble is that it moves from syllable to syllable under the influence of neighbouring short or long vowels or of inflectional changes. For this reason it is often useless to indicate the stress on the basic form of a word as shown in the vocabulary ... particularly when the stress is vital to the meaning, as, for example, in the indefinite form of many nouns' (uhada 'the lion'; hadab 'a lion' vs hadab 'lions' distinguished by stress).

sources.citation: Hudson, R. A. (1973). Syllables, moras and accents in Beja. Journal of Linguistics 9(1): 53-63.
sources.quote: Beja is not a tone-language as this term is normally understood, but has a pitch-accent system in which syllables are either accented or not accented; the position of the accent is unpredictable, as witness: [barra:d] 'tea-pot' [find3a:n] 'coffee-cup' ... The position of an accent is determined by counting back either one 'place' or no 'places' to the left of a fixed point, which thus may or may not itself bear the accent. ... Whether the accent is located on this fixed point or one place before it is determined by a complicated interplay of grammatical and lexical factors, but in many nouns the distinction between singular and plural is made by shifting the accent back one place
sources.locator: §1 p.54 and §2 p.54 (PDF pp.2-3); rule summary §4 p.57, 'In all nouns the accent is on the last mora of the stem' p.58; conclusions §6 pp.62-63
sources.note: Full 11-page paper read (clean ABBYY text layer). Beja has a pitch-accent system (not tone); 'the position of the accent is unpredictable' (p.54, barra:d 'tea-pot' vs finja:n 'coffee-cup'). Placement is computed from a fixed point (for nouns, the last mora of the stem): the accent sits on the fixed point ('final' accent) or one place before it ('penultimate' accent), the choice being 'a complicated interplay of grammatical and lexical factors' (p.54); many nouns mark plural by shifting the accent one place (de:t/de:t, kita:b/kitab, pp.55-56).
